etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English seen, from Old English sēon (“to see, look, behold, perceive, observe, discern, understand, know”), from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”).

definitions.definition: To witness or observe by personal experience.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 8:51, column 1:
quote.text: Uerely, verely I ſay vnto you, If a man keepe my ſaying, hee ſhall neuer ſee death.

quote.citation: 1838 March – 1839 October, Charles Dickens, “Mr. Ralph Nickleby cuts an old Acquaintance. It would also appear from the contents hereof, that a joke, even between Husband and Wife, may be sometimes carried too far.”, in The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby, London: Chapman and Hall, […], published 1839, →OCLC, page 434:
quote.text: […]  And remember this, 'scape-gallows,' said Ralph, menacing him with his hand, 'that if we meet again, and you so much as notice me by one begging gesture, you shall see the inside of a jail once more  […]

definitions.definition: To watch (a movie) at a cinema, or a show on television etc.
(transitive) To perceive or detect someone or something with the eyes, or as if by sight.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC, page 18:
quote.text: Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path. […] It twisted and turned, […] and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn. And, back of the lawn, was a big, old-fashioned house, with piazzas stretching in front of it, and all blazing with lights. 'Twas the house I'd seen the roof of from the beach.

quote.citation: 1959, Georgette Heyer, chapter 1, in The Unknown Ajax:
quote.text: But Richmond […] appeared to lose himself in his own reflections. Some pickled crab, which he had not touched, had been removed with a damson pie; and his sister saw […] that he had eaten no more than a spoonful of that either.

quote.citation: 2016, VOA Learning English (public domain)
quote.text:
I want to see this house!
Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: (figuratively) To understand.

quote.citation: 2013 June 28, Joris Luyendijk, “Our banks are out of control”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 3, page 21:
quote.text: Seeing the British establishment struggle with the financial sector is like watching an alcoholic […] . Until 2008 there was denial over what finance had become. […] But the scandals kept coming […] . A broad section of the political class now recognises the need for change but remains unable to see the necessity of a fundamental overhaul.

definitions.definition: To come to a realization of having been mistaken or misled.
(transitive) To foresee, predict, or prophesy.

quote.citation: 1967, Alan Gordon, Garry Bonner (lyrics and music), “Happy Together”, performed by The Turtles:
quote.text: I can't see me lovin' nobody but you / For all my life / When you're with me, baby the skies'll be blue / For all my life

definitions.definition: (used in the imperative) Used to emphasise a proposition.
To form a mental picture of.

quote.citation: 2013 August 23, Mark Cocker, “Wings of Desire”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 11, page 28:
quote.text: It is not just that we see birds as little versions of ourselves. It is also that, at the same time, they stand outside any moral process. They are utterly indifferent. This absolute oblivion on their part, this lack of sharing, is powerful.

quote.citation: 2014 October 14, David Malcolm, “The Great War Re-Remembered: Allohistory and Allohistorical Fiction”, in Martin Löschnigg, Marzena Sokolowska-Paryz, editors, The Great War in Post-Memory Literature and Film‎[1], Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG., →ISBN, page 173:
quote.text: The question of the plausibility of the counter-factual is seen as key in all three discussions of allohistorical fiction (as it is in Demandt's and Ferguson's examinations of allohistory) (cf. Rodiek 25–26; Ritter 15–16; Helbig 32).

definitions.definition: To have an interview with; especially, to make a call upon; to visit.

definitions.definition: To date frequently.

quote.text: "You're... remarrying?  I didn't even know you were seeing someone.  And she's going to live here?"

definitions.definition: To visit for a medical appointment.
(social) To meet, to visit.
(ergative) To be the setting or time of.

quote.text: It seems as if every passing year sees the mainstream embrace a longtime cult-favorite alternative rock band.

definitions.definition: (by extension) Chiefly followed by that: to ensure that something happens, especially by personally witnessing it.

quote.citation: 2001, Joan Lock, Death in Perspective, London: Robert Hale, →ISBN, page 52:
quote.text: 'Don't worry. You won't lose out. I'll see you get your share of the action. If not now, later.'

quote.citation: 2022 October 27, Brian Porter, “The last barrel of oil should be a Canadian one”, in The Globe and Mail‎[2], Toronto, ON: The Woodbridge Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2022-12-17:
quote.text: We have forgotten that such a transition will require compromise, as we address real energy needs today, and investment, as we adapt to cleaner ways of producing energy tomorrow. A well-managed transition will see that the opportunities flowing from the transformation dramatically exceed these costs.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To wait upon; attend, escort.

quote.citation: 2020, Rich Thompson, Jonny Robinson (lyrics and music), “Your Will Be Done”‎[3]:
quote.text: And in this Name we overcome, for You shall see us safely home.

definitions.definition: (gambling, transitive) To respond to another player's bet with a bet of equal value.
To determine by trial or experiment; to find out (if or whether).
(used in the imperative) To reference or to study for further details.
To examine something closely, or to utilize something, often as a temporary alternative.
To include as one of something's experiences.
Introducing an explanation

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English se, see, from Old French sie (“seat, throne; town, capital; episcopal see”), from Latin sedes (“seat”), referring to the bishop's throne or chair (compare seat of power) in the cathedral; related to the Latin verb sedere (“to sit”).

definitions.definition: A diocese, archdiocese; a region of a church, generally headed by a bishop or an archbishop.
The office of a bishop or archbishop.
A seat; a site; a place where sovereign power is exercised.

quote.text: Ioue laught on Venus from his ſouerayne ſee

definitions.definition: Alternative form of cee; the name of the Latin-script letter C/c.
